t: Introduction: norms of morality and law
n: We begin this topic with the norms of morality and law. The relations of people in society with one another, including in professional activity, are governed by social norms. Moral norms arise in a "natural" way, and their observance is secured by the force of public opinion. Legal norms, in turn, are introduced by the state, and their observance is secured by state compulsion. That is, the difference is that in morality public opinion acts, whereas in law there stands state compulsion.

Official documents made up of legal norms are called normative legal acts. They take the form of a law or subordinate acts. Subordinate acts include a Presidential decree, resolution, government resolution and others. In the sphere of health care these are the orders, instructions, rules and regulations of the Ministry of Health. This means that the documents regulating the doctor's activity form a whole system, from the law to the ministry's instructions.

Now we turn to the main concept: professional offences of medical workers, abbreviated POMW. The activity of medical workers is defined by law and other normative documents. The logic is simple: a normative requirement exists, and the worker does not fulfil it or fulfils it improperly. Failure to fulfil, or improper fulfilment of, the established requirements is called a POMW.

According to the theory of law, an offence has five features. The first is the act, that is, an action or omission. The second is social danger, that is, the feature of danger to society. The third is unlawfulness, that is, contradiction of the law. The fourth is fault, that is, the guilt of the person. The fifth is an unfavourable consequence, that is, the occurrence of harm or danger. Remember: to speak of an offence, these features are considered together.

t: Distinction between a misdemeanour and a crime
n: By social danger, a POMW may be a misdemeanour or a crime. If an unlawful act does not have the feature of social danger and is not provided for in the Criminal Code, it is called a misdemeanour. If the act has features of social danger, it is assessed as a crime. In both cases the act is unlawful; the difference is determined by the presence or absence of features of social danger.

t: Types of misdemeanours of medical workers
n: From the standpoint of law, the misdemeanours of medical workers are divided into disciplinary, administrative and civil. A disciplinary misdemeanour means violation of the established order of labour, service and production. In an administrative misdemeanour the order of administration of the institution is violated. In a civil misdemeanour, property and non-property rights are violated. That is, we distinguish each type by what is being violated.

An administrative offence relates chiefly to violation of the order of administration of a particular institution. A civil misdemeanour means violation of the property and non-property rights of citizens and organisations. As the table shows: in a disciplinary misdemeanour the order of labour, service and production is violated; in an administrative one, the order of administration of the institution; in a civil one, property and non-property rights. The essence of these offences and the liability for them are set out in detail in the later chapters of the textbook.

t: Specific features of the doctor's activity
n: Besides misdemeanours, there is a group of unfavourable outcomes called medical error and accident. The reason lies in the specific nature of the doctor's activity: the doctor works with the most complex object in nature, that is, the human being, and problems arise that have no standard solution. Remember: medical error and accident are not legal concepts, and do not appear in legislative acts. A misdemeanour, however, may be disciplinary, administrative or civil.

Errare humanum est, that is, in Latin: to err is human. The activity of medical workers is no exception. To be free of error is a very difficult matter, and in assessing medical error there are opposing views. The phrase "medical error" was first proposed by N. I. Pirogov. That is why the history of attitudes to this concept also begins with the name of this scientist.

t: Pirogov and Billroth: attitude to error
n: Let us compare two views on the attitude to error. Pirogov stressed that the doctor has the right to make mistakes but has no right to conceal them. In 1837 he regarded speaking openly about one's activity and its results as a sacred duty. Billroth, for his part, said: only the faint-hearted fear to speak openly about errors. This means that both scientists were in favour of not concealing an error.

Davydovsky in 1928 gave a definition of medical error: a medical error is a doctor's conscientious mistake. Its causes: the imperfection of medical science and methods, an atypical course of the disease, or insufficient training of the doctor. It is important that in such an error there are no elements of coldness, inattention or medical negligence. That is, if there is negligence, it is no longer a matter of a conscientious mistake.

A "medical error", from the legal point of view, should not mean a crime, or an administrative, disciplinary or civil misdemeanour. The consequences of a "conscientious mistake" should, logically, not give rise to legal liability. At the same time, they should be disclosed and discussed among colleagues so as not to be repeated. The chain is as follows: a medical error, legal liability does not arise, the error is disclosed, then it is discussed among colleagues.

Davydovsky paid particular attention to studying medical errors and eliminating them in the work of other doctors. His definition dates from 1928. The first clinico-anatomical conference was held on 9 December 1930 at the "Medsantrud" hospital in Moscow. That is, the practice of openly discussing errors began to be established through these conferences.

Now we shall look at case analyses. First case: a man of about 30 presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and one loose stool. Blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 90. The doctor suspected food poisoning and decided to wash out the stomach. During insertion of the tube the patient suddenly died. At autopsy an acute myocardial infarction was found: this is the abdominal form of infarction.

The second case dates from 1870. Krassovsky removed an ovarian cyst, and after 40 hours the young woman died. On pathoanatomical examination it was found that a sponge swab had been left in the abdominal cavity. Krassovsky regarded it as a duty to describe the case in a journal. He also proposed counting the sponges and attaching long tapes to them. That is, the error was named openly and a conclusion was drawn from it so that it would not be repeated.

The third case dates from 1886. Kolomnin operated on a woman for an ulcer of the rectum. For anaesthesia an enema of cocaine was given, 4 times 6 grains, that is 1.5 g. About 45 min after the operation her condition deteriorated sharply, the patient died after 3 hours, and cocaine poisoning was confirmed. The persecution of the doctor ended in tragedy: 5 days after the operation, on 11 November 1886, Kolomnin killed himself.

Now the concept of accident. An accident is the outcome of chance circumstances independent of the medical worker, which could not have been foreseen or prevented. In most cases such outcomes occur as a result of individual features of organs that were not detected during life. Remember: the main feature here is that the medical worker had no possibility of foreseeing and preventing it.

We give examples of accident. The first is idiosyncrasy to some ordinary drugs, or the later development of hypersensitivity to drugs taken earlier. The second is rupture of an aneurysm of the cerebral vessels, which had been asymptomatic, during an ordinary procedure. The third is reflex cardiac arrest during angiography or gastrofibroscopy. The fourth is sudden death from psycho-emotional shock on the eve of an operation.

In an accident the outcome does not depend on the doctor's action or omission. Therefore an accident cannot give rise to any form of liability of the medical worker. However, like a medical error, the consequences of an accident must necessarily be studied and analysed in the medical institution. That is, although there is no liability, analysis is mandatory.

The term "iatrogenesis" was proposed in 1925 by the German psychiatrist O. Bumke. The term comes from the Greek words iatros, that is doctor, and gennao, that is I produce. Originally, iatrogenesis meant illnesses arising from the unfavourable effect of the doctor's words or actions on the patient's psyche. Kassirsky in 1970 proposed including in it also incorrect performance of procedures and incorrect use of drugs.

Iatrogenesis can sometimes be committed by mid-level medical staff. In this connection the Hungarian psychotherapist I. Hardi in 1972 proposed the term "sororigenesis" for the consequences of the actions of nurses. The term comes from the Latin soror, that is sister. This means that iatrogenesis may relate not only to the doctor but also to the actions of the nurse.

Authors characterise iatrogenesis in different ways. Some include in it all professional offences, others only cases of negligence. The preferred definition is as follows: iatrogenesis is the causing of harm to the patient's health in connection with diagnosis, treatment, prevention or rehabilitation. This definition is cited under the names of Sergeev and Erofeev.

According to the generally accepted interpretation, iatrogenesis is a new pathological condition arising under the influence of medical factors. A medical factor includes all elements of medical technology. In addition, the conditions of the treatment and preventive institution in which the patient was staying are also regarded as a medical factor. That is, the factor is not only the doctor's action but also the conditions of the institution.

The types of iatrogenesis are as follows: diagnostic, therapeutic, psycho-emotional and informational, preventive, non-therapeutic and others. Therapeutic iatrogenesis includes therapeutic, surgical and physical types. Non-therapeutic, in turn, means late presentation for medical care. This classification shows that iatrogenesis can arise at different stages and in different forms.

The consequences of a professional offence may be interpreted as manifestations of iatrogenesis. Such consequences include crime, misdemeanour, medical error and accident. That is, iatrogenesis is a broad concept that may unite all four of the cases considered above.

The most serious manifestation of a professional offence of medical workers is a crime. Features of a crime: danger to society, criminal unlawfulness, guilt, and the provision of punishment. A crime is a culpably committed, socially dangerous act prohibited by the Criminal Code under threat of punishment. This is established by Article 14 of the Criminal Code. Fault takes the form of intent or negligence.

A person who committed an act intentionally or through negligence may be found guilty, as stated in Article 20 of the Criminal Code. In direct intent, the person was aware of the danger, foresaw the consequences and desired their occurrence. In indirect intent, the person foresaw the consequences and consciously allowed their occurrence, as given in Article 21 of the Criminal Code. That is, the difference lies in the attitude to the consequence: in one case the person desires it, in the other he consciously allows it.

There are two kinds of negligence. In self-confidence, the person foresees the possibility of the consequence but, without observing precautions, groundlessly hopes that it will not occur. In carelessness, the person did not foresee the consequence although he should and could have foreseen it, as stated in Article 22 of the Criminal Code. Remember: in most cases medical workers are held liable for crimes committed through negligence.

Let us look at examples of negligence. A surgeon and anaesthetist on duty, without reason, without preparation, and without an assistant or operating nurse, performed an elective abdominal operation. This is a case of self-confidence. In the second example the doctor did not carry out the current standards; the investigation established that he was not familiar with the standards although he should have known them. This is a case of carelessness.

t: Circumstances excluding the criminality of an act
n: There are circumstances that exclude the criminality of an act. These are justified professional risk and extreme necessity. Extreme necessity is defined as follows: if the danger could not be eliminated by other means, and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, there is no crime. This is established by Article 38 of the Criminal Code. Justified risk relates to Article 41 of the Criminal Code.

t: Examples of extreme necessity and justified risk
n: Example: in laryngospasm, a doctor outside an institution made a tracheostomy with the means at hand. Life was saved, purulent complications then occurred, but this is not a crime. A risk is regarded as justified if it accords with modern knowledge and experience, the aim could not be achieved without risk, and the harm was prevented; this is in Article 41 of the Criminal Code. A risk taken in the knowledge of the danger that people may perish, however, is not recognised as justified.

The next case concerns a cardiac wound. A patient with a stab-incised wound of the chest came to a district hospital, and damage to the heart was found. There are no conditions for cardiac surgery, the patient cannot be transferred, and calling a cardiac surgeon was also useless. The surgeon on duty decided to suture the cardiac wound. This is the only correct decision, the professional risk is justified, and the act is not a crime.

Criminal liability arises only when a person has committed a socially dangerous act intentionally or through negligence. Criminal liability is established for sane natural persons. In most cases these are persons who have reached 16 at the time of the crime, as stated in Article 17 of the Criminal Code. Insanity, in turn, arises when medical and legal criteria are present.

The features of a criminal act established by law are called the corpus delicti. It has elements. The object is usually the health and life of citizens. The objective side consists of the act, the consequence and the causal connection between them. The subject is a natural person: more often a doctor, sometimes mid-level and junior staff; officials may also be subjects.

t: Groups of crimes of medical workers
n: The crimes of medical workers fall into three groups. Crimes against health and life: negligent homicide, 102; bodily injury, 104, 105, 109, 111; abortion, 114; failure to perform duties, 116; leaving in danger, 117. Against the order of administration: official forgery, Article 209; taking a bribe, Article 210; giving a bribe, Article 211. Against public safety: violation of sanitary or anti-epidemic rules, Article 257, and violation of the rules for handling narcotic drugs, Article 275.

t: Article 116 of the Criminal Code: improper performance of duties
n: Article 116 of the Criminal Code is devoted to improper performance of duties. If failure to perform professional duty through carelessness or dishonesty causes injury of moderate severity or grave injury, criminal liability arises. If a person obliged to give assistance fails, without a valid reason, to give it and this causes injury of moderate severity or grave injury, a more severe penalty is provided. If through negligence it causes the death of people or other grave consequences, a still more severe penalty is provided.

Under Article 30 of the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health", medical and pharmaceutical workers are obliged to give emergency assistance. In cases of necessity, assistance must be given regardless of place and time. This applies also outside the medical institution and outside working hours. That is, a doctor cannot refuse assistance on the ground that he is not at his workplace.

The reasons for failing to give assistance may be valid or invalid. Valid reasons: the worker's illness, being occupied with a more severe patient, the absence of drugs, instruments, equipment or transport, natural disasters. Not considered valid: days off and holidays, non-working time, leave, lack of special knowledge in an emergency, personal enmity toward the patient. The question of whether the reasons are valid is decided by the court.

t: Vermel: three conditions for criminal liability
n: Vermel indicated three conditions for criminal liability. First: the worker's actions are objectively wrong and contrary to official instructions, rules and standards. Second: the worker, in accordance with his training and category, must be aware that his actions are wrong and must have a real possibility of making the correct decision. Third: the action or omission must have a direct causal connection with serious unfavourable consequences.

t: Criminal abortion (Article 114 of the Criminal Code)
n: Criminal abortion is provided for in Article 114 of the Criminal Code. Under the first part, liability arises if an obstetrician-gynaecologist performs an artificial termination of pregnancy outside treatment institutions or where it is medically impossible. The second part relates to the carrying out of such work by a person with no right to perform an artificial termination of pregnancy. That is, the first part relates to the obstetrician-gynaecologist, and the second to a person with no right.
